questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How banks make their profits from customers' savings
How to pay for a TV licence online or by phone
How to choose a strong password for your accounts
How criminals trick people out of money, often online
questions.why: Sam and Rob discuss fraud and the methods criminals use, much of it online.

questions.q: What did thousands of people in the UK fall for this year?
options: A fake email about paying their TV licence
A phone call from a fake bank manager
A letter about winning a prize
A fake online shop
questions.why: Rob mentions a fraudulent email asking people to update their TV licence direct debit.

questions.q: What does Shari Vahl say about the fake email she has?
options: It had lots of spelling mistakes and odd grammar
It was rude and threatening, asking for money fast
It looked real, with the right logos and fonts
It asked for a very large payment within a day
questions.why: She says it looks completely convincing, with all the right logos and fonts.

questions.q: What does Shari Vahl mean by 'look over there whilst they rifle your pockets'?
options: Criminals steal from people in crowds
Criminals distract you while they steal from you
People should always check their pockets
Criminals work in pairs
questions.why: Rob says she means it metaphorically, as a sleight of hand trick.

questions.q: What is 'phishing', as explained in the programme?
options: Stealing money from a cash machine using a hidden camera
Hacking into someone's computer with a dangerous virus
Emailing as if from your bank to get private details
Calling people at home to sell them products they don't need
questions.why: Sam says it's sending an email that looks like it came from your bank.

questions.q: According to Jenny Radcliffe, what do criminals look for?
options: A small piece of personal information to build on
People with a lot of money in their savings accounts
Old computers that are easy to hack into from abroad
Bank staff who are willing to help them for a fee
questions.why: She says they look for 'a key that unlocks just a small part' of someone's identity.

questions.q: How does Jenny Radcliffe describe what happens in a good fraud?
options: It is over very quickly, usually in minutes
It only takes small amounts of money each time
It is easy to spot if you are careful
It keeps building until the results are devastating
questions.why: She says it will 'build and build and build' until the consequences are devastating.

questions.q: What advice do banks give, according to Rob?
options: Only use cash, and avoid cards and online banking
Don't give bank details online; change passwords often
Never open any emails from people you don't know
Keep your savings at home instead of in a bank account
questions.why: Rob says banks warn us not to give away details online and to change passwords regularly.
